teaser:

title: KELLI O'HARA - DIRECT FROM BROADWAY
teaser:
Kelli O'Hara has established herself as one of Broadway's greatest leading ladies. The Tony Award winner, Emmy, SAG, and Grammy-nominated actress has appeared in twelve Broadway shows for which she has garnered eight Tony Award nominations. 

She won the 2015 Tony Award for Best Leading Actress in a Musical, along with Grammy, Drama League and Outer Critics nominations for her portrayal of Anna Leonowens in The King and I. O’Hara’s other Broadway credits include Kiss Me Kate, The Bridges of Madison County, Nice Work if You Can Get It, South Pacific, The Pajama Game, The Light in the Piazza, Sweet Smell of Success, Follies, Dracula, and Jekyll & Hyde. 

O’Hara received an Emmy Award nomination for her portrayal of Katie Bonner in Topic's hit web series, The Accidental Wolf, and can currently be seen on HBO’s The Gilded Age, which was nominated for a SAG award for Outstanding Performance by an Ensemble in a Drama Series for Season 2. Additional film and television credits include Showtime's Master of Sex, 13 Reasons Why, Blue Bloods, All My Children, All the Bright Places, Peter Pan Live!, Sex & The City 2, Martin Scorsese's The Key to Reserva, The Good Fight, N3mbers, and Car Talk. 

In 2015, she made history as the first artist to make the crossover from Broadway to Opera when she made her Metropolitan Opera debut in Lehar's The Merry Widow opposite Renee Fleming and in 2018 returned as Despina in Mozart's Cosi Fan Tutte. She was last seen at The Metropolitan Opera in the world premiere of Kevin Puts’, The Hours, as Laura Brown, which earned a Grammy nomination for Best Opera Recording. 

O’Hara is a frequent performer on PBS's live telecasts, The Kennedy Center Honors, and performs often alongside The New York Philharmonic and The New York Pops. Along with her two Grammy nominations, her solo albums, Always and Wonder in the World, are available on Ghostlight. 

O’Hara recently completed a critically-acclaimed limited Broadway engagement of the new musical Days of Wine and Roses, which also garnered rave reviews during its Off-Broadway run at The Atlantic Theatre Company. She won the Outer Critics Circle Award and the Drama Desk Award for Outstanding Lead Performer in a Broadway Musical in addition to receiving Tony and Drama League Nominations for her role.

Next spring, she will return to Broadway in the play, Fallen Angels.

Discover a world of imagination, where music, movement, and art reveal the beauty and wonder of some of our planet’s most extraordinary animals.

Carnival of the Nearly Extinct Animals is a visually captivating, multidisciplinary performance celebrating some of the planet’s most rare and remarkable creatures. Through a seamless blend of live music, dance, and larger-than-life puppetry, audiences are invited on an unforgettable journey into the beauty of the natural world.

Presented by Ocean Music Action in partnership with Hawaiʻi Theatre Center, this World Premiere performance features newly commissioned choreography by Dance Heginbotham with dancers of Ballet Hawaiʻi, performed alongside an evocative live musical score. Large-scale animal puppetry by Obie Award–winning puppeteer Greg Corbino brings each creature to life with striking detail and expressive storytelling.

Original poetry by local students is woven throughout the performance, offering a poignant reflection on connection, care, and our shared responsibility for the future of these animals. Bringing together internationally recognized artists and leading local creatives, Carnival of the Nearly Extinct Animals is a feast for the senses and a powerful call to action— an unforgettable theatrical experience for audiences of all ages.

title: A TASTE OF IRELAND
teaser:
Direct from Off-Broadway and London’s West End , the internationally acclaimed A Taste of Ireland Company brings its flagship production — ‘A Taste of Ireland — The Irish Music Dance Sensation’ to Hawaii for the first time. Laugh, cry, and jig into the night with production that is Celtic, for this generation. 

Performed by former World Irish dance champions, and featuring dancers from Lord of the Dance, Riverdance, and the recent West End cast of Éireann, ‘A Taste of Ireland’ brings the spirit and energy of modern Ireland to life with a pint of Irish wit. Watch world-class performers blend melodic folk mash-ups, live jaw-dropping acapella tap battles, and heartfelt storytelling in a live celebration of Irish music and dance. 

Featuring revamped classics of Danny Boy, Tell Me Ma, Wild Rover, and many more well-known songs, the show’s reimagined contemporary score blossoms alongside the brash Irish charm of the live dance cast. ‘A Taste of Ireland’ merges cultural traditions, modern flaie and craic galore to deliver a performance that has been leaving audiences across the globe jigging on their feet for the last decade.

With a social media following of over 300,000, ‘A Taste of Ireland’ is exactly what it promises: a taste of everything you love about Ireland — with a generous helping of more.‘A Taste of Ireland’ is a show with 100% live singing and dancing that fuses storytelling, modern Irish dance, tap, and contemporary performance to bring Ireland’s stories to life on stage. 

With a strictly limited touring schedule, see ‘A Taste of Ireland’ before it takes off around the globe once again. 

Witness the birth of a nation told through rhythm and beat, with the cry of the Vikings as they were brought to defeat, the rise and fall of the rebellion the show tells the tale, trapped were the Irish, watch them dance from the jail. For the nation fought free from Dundalk to Tralee, they sing and they dance through the night full of glee. For Ireland, there was not a nation quite like her, hold onto your seat, feel Ireland’s passion and fire.

title: 'Ainakea
teaser:
Maui OnStage presents the 3rd production of our 2026 Season - 'Ainakea.

Written by Maui playwright - James Nevius

Directed by Francis Tau'a

Dates: Oct 2 - 18

Times: Fri at 7:30pm, Sat & Sun at 3pm

Historic Iao Theater in Wailuku

Tickets: $10 - $45

  
  


ʻAinakea is set on Maui’s west side in 1953. The play tells the fictional story of the wealthy Goodale family and their failing sugar plantation, ‘Ainakea, which was named for a type of prized white sugarcane.

The play is an adaptation of Anton Chekhov’s classic drama The Cherry Orchard, widely considered one of the great plays of the early 20th century. Nevius has updated the drama to the 1950s. With statehood looming and the traditional, plantation-based sugar business coming to an end, this was a period of great uncertainty and change in the Hawaiian islands.

Nevius' last full-length play, Murder in the Nth Degree, won the ProArts Playhouse inaugural playwriting competition and was named Best Play of 2022 by Broadway World Hawaiʻi.

Set along the stunning Kohala Coast, this play-and-eat golf experience brings together golfers, chefs, and community leaders for an unforgettable day on one of Hawaiʻi’s most iconic seaside courses!

“Putt” your appetite to the test as you stop by chef stations along the green serving fresh, local flavors from Hawai‘i Island’s top culinary talents. title: Smoked, Shucked & Cured
teaser:
Fire, salt, smoke, and sea—these elements shape some of the world’s most beloved culinary traditions! Join us at the breathtaking Mauna Kea Beach Hotel for Smoked, Shucked and Cured, a grand tasting where you’ll discover the bold flavors and craftsmanship behind these timeless techniques.

Ten masterful chefs gather along on the Island of Hawaiʻi to showcase dishes inspired by the art of smoking, shucking, and curing—from flame-kissed meats and delicately cured specialties to the ocean’s freshest seafood served straight from the shell. With each bite, you’ll experience the vibrant bounty of Hawaiʻi as land and sea come together through time-honored methods and modern culinary creativity.

Every smoky, savory, and briny bite is complemented by world-class wines, craft cocktails, and refreshing brews, thoughtfully selected and crafted by award-winning wine professionals and mixologists. From crisp mineral-driven wines to spirits kissed with smoke, you’ll sip your way through pairings that highlight the depth and character of Hawaii’s extraordinary ingredients.

Join us under the stars along the Kohala Coast for an unforgettable evening celebrating the flavors of Hawaiʻi from land to sea.

title: No EGGScuses, Let’s Brunch!
teaser:

From farm-fresh hen eggs to delicate quail eggs and glistening pearls of roe, this playful brunch explores the many delicious ways chefs around the world elevate this culinary staple.

Six talented chefs crack open their creativity with a lineup of dishes showcasing eggs in all their glorious forms—poached, fried, scrambled, baked, cured, and more. From savory brunch classics to inventive chef-driven bites, each dish highlights the vibrant flavors of Hawaiʻi’s incredible locally grown, raised, and caught ingredients.

Pair your plate with rosé, brunch-ready cocktails, and refreshing sips crafted by talented mixologists while you soak in the ocean breeze and easygoing Sunday vibes. Whether you’re here for silky yolks, luxurious roe, or sweet morning indulgences, this walk-around brunch is sure to leave you feeling egg-static.

title: FEAST Summit
teaser:
FEAST Summit is Hawaiʻi’s premier one-day professional development conference at the intersection of Food, Education, Agriculture, Sustainability, and Tourism. Bringing together global and local leaders—from chefs, restaurateurs, and hoteliers to farmers, educators, food and beverage innovators, and policymakers—FEAST offers a full day of insights, collaboration, and forward-looking dialogue shaping the future of food systems and travel.

Designed as a catalyst for connection and impact, this full system-wide conversation—from farm to table to travel—brings together generations of industry experts to share knowledge, exchange ideas, and help shape Hawaiʻi’s future. Created for industry professionals, emerging talent, and students alike, FEAST delivers both perspective and practical value through expert-led sessions, dynamic discussions, and curated networking—offering direct access to decision-makers and innovators from Hawaiʻi and across the U.S.

What to Expect:

  * 50+ global speakers and local luminaries sharing expertise across Hawaii’s culinary, hospitality, agriculture, and visitor industries



  * Dozens of timely conversations spanning regenerative agriculture and value-added production, AAPI identity and the future of American cuisine, culinary tourism and the role of food in driving experiences, the rise of private dining, advancing women’s leadership in culinary and hospitality, and so much more!



  * Unmatched access to industry leaders—expand your network with decision-makers and innovators from the Continental U.S., Hawaiʻi and beyond.



  * Nonna Knows Best Presented by HMAA—a curated grand tasting lunch experience featuring eight chefs celebrating culinary heritage and traditions passed down through generations, bringing the conversations of the day to life through food




Why Attend:  


Stay ahead of industry trends, build meaningful connections, and gain actionable insights to grow your business, advance your career, and contribute to a more resilient and innovative food system.

title: Culture in AgriCULTURE Presented by Kamehameha Schools
teaser:
Step into the loʻi and reconnect with the land at Culture in AgriCULTURE Presented by Kamehameha Schools, an immersive day bringing food, farming, and culture together at Kākoʻo ʻŌiwi. Rooted in the belief that agriculture is inseparable from culture, this one-of-a-kind experience invites you to engage directly with the practices that have sustained communities for generations.

Begin with a hands-on experience in the loʻi, learning about the cultivation of kalo and the deep cultural significance of ahupuaʻa system (a traditional Hawaiian land management system). Guided by stewards of the land, you’ll gain insight into how ancestral knowledge continues to shape Hawaii’s food systems today.

Then gather for a family-style lunch prepared by acclaimed Indigenous chefs from around the world, sharing the flavors and stories of their respective heritage foodways while highlighting the connection between culture, identity, and what we grow and eat. The day culminates in a panel discussion where chefs and cultural practitioners explore how Indigenous foodways can inspire more resilient and sustainable food systems—sharing how they are preserving traditional knowledge, strengthening food sovereignty, and reconnecting communities to the land.

Join us for a day of learning, sharing, and connection—where culture lives in the soil, on the plate, and in the stories we carry forward.

Note: As this event takes place outdoors and includes a hands-on experience, guests are encouraged to wear work-ready casual attire, including comfortable clothing and closed-toe shoes or flip-flops. Please come prepared for sun, water, and muddy conditions, and consider bringing sun protection, bug spray, a towel, and a change of clothes.

title: BTS: Beyond the Seoul
teaser:
Experience an evening where heritage, innovation, and global influence converge at the Hawaiʻi Food & Wine Festival’s annual Halekulani Gala. This year, BTS: Beyond the Seoul invites guests to explore the evolution of Korean cuisine—where deep-rooted traditions meet modern culinary artistry in an extraordinary expression of culture, craft, and creativity.

Five world-class chefs—among the most celebrated voices in contemporary Korean gastronomy—present a five-course wine-paired dinner that explores the foundations of hansik through a refined, modern lens. Rooted in centuries-old traditions of fermentation, seasonality, and balance, each course reflects the philosophies that have shaped Korean cuisine, while showcasing the innovation that has propelled it onto the world stage.

Paired with a curated selection of ultra-luxury wines, every course is a study in precision and harmony—thoughtfully composed, technically masterful, and deeply expressive. From the quiet depth of aged flavors to the vibrant energy of modern interpretation, the evening unfolds as a journey beyond the plate—into the soul of a cuisine defined by both tradition and transformation.

Join us for an unforgettable night that honors heritage, celebrates culinary excellence, and brings the spirit of Korea to life through a truly world-class dining experience.

title: Nā Wāhine O Ke Kai World Championship Race
teaser:
Nā Wāhine O Ke Kai World Championship

Celebrate the strength, heritage, and sisterhood of outrigger canoe paddling as the world’s elite female athletes take on the legendary Kaiwi Channel.

Known as the "Women of the Sea,"  Nā Wāhine O Ke Kai is universally revered as the premier women’s outrigger canoe race in the world. This grueling 41-to-42-mile journey begins at the historic Hale O Lono Harbor on Molokaʻi and finishes on the shores of Waikīkī, Oʻahu.

Paddlers face the treacherous Kaiwi Channel—a notoriously unpredictable stretch of open ocean known for its massive swells, powerful currents, and relentless winds. Crossing it requires months of intense physical preparation, precise open-ocean navigation, and absolute synchronization among the six-woman crew.

Since its groundbreaking inception in 1979, this race has been far more than an elite athletic competition. It is a powerful celebration of Hawaiian culture, ancestral traditions, and women’s empowerment. The event fosters a deep sense of global ʻohana (family) and camaraderie, uniting paddlers from Hawaiʻi and across the globe in a shared pursuit of excellence, resilience, and aloha.

 Event Quick Facts

  * The Route: Hale O Lono, Molokaʻi to Duke Kahanamoku Beach, Waikīkī, Oʻahu.

  * The Distance: 41–42 miles of challenging open ocean.

  * The Mission: Honoring the past, perpetuating Hawaiian culture, and showcasing the pinnacle of women’s strength and teamwork.




Join us in cheering on these incredible athletes as they honor tradition and conquer the ocean!

title: Molokaʻi Hoe World Championship Race
teaser:
Molokaʻi Hoe World Championship Canoe Race

Witness the ultimate test of physical endurance, mental fortitude, and ocean mastery as the world’s best male outrigger canoe paddlers battle the infamous Kaiwi Channel.

The Men's World Championship

Since its historic inception in 1952, the Molokaʻi Hoe has stood as the most prestigious men's outrigger canoe race in the world. This grueling 41-mile open-ocean marathon launches from Hale O Lono Harbor on the island of Molokaʻi and culminates on the iconic shores of Duke Kahanamoku Beach in Waikīkī, Oʻahu.

Crews must navigate the unpredictable and punishing waters of the Kaiwi Channel—a stretch of ocean notorious for towering swells, fierce trade winds, and shifting currents. It takes unparalleled teamwork, strategic navigation, and raw stamina to conquer the elements and reach the finish line.

Honoring Ancient Traditions

More than just a race, the Molokaʻi Hoe is a vibrant celebration of Hawaiian heritage. It honors the ancient Polynesian navigators and the deep-rooted cultural significance of the waʻa (canoe). Each year, the event draws over 1,000 elite paddlers from around the globe, uniting international competitors in a shared spirit of aloha, mutual respect, and reverence for the ocean.

Event Quick Facts

  * The Route: Hale O Lono, Molokaʻi to Duke Kahanamoku Beach, Waikīkī, Oʻahu.

  * The Distance: ~41 miles across the treacherous Kaiwi Channel.

  * The Legacy: Running continuously since 1952, perpetuating the strength and tradition of Hawaiian outrigger canoe racing.




Experience the power, passion, and pride as these incredible crews carry a legacy across the sea!

title: 'Ulu Festival
teaser:
The ʻUlu Festival is a public, community-rooted celebration of ʻulu (breadfruit) as a foundational Native Hawaiian food, cultural kinolau, and climate-resilient agroforestry crop. Hosted at the Amy B.H. Greenwell Ethnobotanical Garden in Kona, the festival is designed to elevate ʻike kūpuna, strengthen connection to ʻāina, and inspire restoration of traditional food systems through hands-on learning, cultural demonstration, and community gathering.

By centering ʻulu as both ancestral staple and contemporary food security solution, the festival advances community well-being through the revitalization of traditional food systems and strengthened relationships between people and place.

This free, public event will feature Chef Demonstrations, Grower & Agroforestry Education, Cultural & Ethnobotanical Exhibitors, Keiki Programming, and an ‘Ulu Mākeke (marketplace) featuring value-added producers, artisans, and makers. A breadfruit tree sale will include new varieties not previously available in Hawai‘i!

The 'Ulu Festival is the kickoff event for the 2026 ‘Ulu Ho‘olaule‘a or Breadfruit Celebration - an international week-long series of events honoring breadfruit ('ulu), one of Oceania's most important ancestral crops and an increasingly recognized solution for climate resilience, regenerative agriculture, and community food security. Other Ho‘olaule‘a events include an ‘Aha ‘Ulu September 20-21, the Global Breadfruit Summit on September 22-24 and an ‘Ulu Culinary Showcase on September 23. 

Hosted in the historic Kaluʻulu breadfruit belt of South Kona, where nearly 18 contiguous square miles of breadfruit agroforestry once produced an estimated 35 million pounds of ʻulu annually, the celebration brings together farmers, researchers, Indigenous knowledge holders, educators, chefs, food entrepreneurs, policymakers, students, and community leaders from across Hawaiʻi, the Pacific, and beyond.

Together, we'll explore how traditional knowledge and modern innovation can strengthen food systems for generations to come.

teaser:
Experience the warmth of Hawaiian hospitality through an intimate cultural workshop led by Aunty Kela, a respected kūpuna (elder) and lifelong practitioner of Hawaiian music, hula, and storytelling. More than a performance, this interactive experience invites guests to become participants in the living traditions of Hawaiʻi.

The workshop begins with introductions to the cultural significance of mele (song), hula, and the ʻukulele in Hawaiian life. Guests will learn how music and dance have long served as ways to preserve history, honor loved ones, celebrate special occasions, and strengthen connections between people and place.

Participants are then guided through the basics of playing the ʻukulele, learning proper hand positioning, simple chords, and rhythmic strumming patterns. Whether someone has never held an instrument before or already has musical experience, the lesson is designed to be approachable, engaging, and enjoyable for all skill levels. Together, the group will learn to play a beloved Hawaiian song while gaining an appreciation for the role of music in Hawaiian culture.

The experience continues with an introduction to hula, where Aunty Kela teaches the meanings behind foundational movements and demonstrates how hula tells stories through graceful, intentional motion. Guests learn a simple choreography that corresponds with the song they have just practiced, creating a meaningful connection between music, language, and dance.

Throughout the workshop, Aunty Kela shares personal stories, cultural insights, and the values of aloha, mālama (to care for), and provides guests with a deeper understanding of Hawaiʻi beyond its scenic beauty. Her welcoming teaching style encourages laughter, participation, and genuine cultural exchange, creating an atmosphere that is both educational and memorable.

By the conclusion of the workshop, participants will have learned the basics of playing the ʻukulele, experienced the storytelling tradition of hula, and gained a greater appreciation for the living culture of Hawaiʻi. Guests leave not only with new skills, but with meaningful memories and a deeper connection to the people, traditions, and spirit of these islands.

title: Talk Story & Mākeke
teaser:
As part of the Courtyard by Marriott Oʻahu North Shore's recurring Talk Story & Mākeke series, the hotel invites guests into an evening of authentic Hawaiian storytelling, cultural knowledge, and meaningful conversation. Hosted alongside a vibrant marketplace featuring local artisans, food vendors, and cultural practitioners, this Talk Story session offers visitors a unique opportunity to experience Hawaiʻi through the voice and perspective of respected kūpuna (elders) and community members.

Rooted in the Hawaiian tradition of sharing knowledge through conversation, the Talk Story sessions blend personal experiences, family history, cultural teachings, and humor to create an engaging and welcoming atmosphere. Rather than a formal lecture, each session unfolds naturally, allowing stories to inspire discussion and encourage genuine connections between guests and the local community.

Guests gain a deeper understanding of everyday life in Hawaiʻi, the significance of preserving cultural traditions, and the ways in which ʻike kūpuna (ancestral knowledge) continues to guide communities today. Drawing from a lifetime of lived experience, speakers offers perspectives that cannot be found in guidebooks, creating a memorable and authentic cultural exchange.

Audience participation is encouraged throughout the session, allowing guests to ask questions and engage directly with speakers. Discussions may include Hawaiian and Polynesian customs and traditions, music and hula, family life, language, historical events, and the importance of caring for both people and place. Because every audience is different, each Talk Story becomes a unique experience shaped by curiosity, conversation, and shared learning.

Held in conjunction with the Hau'oli Mākeke marketplace, guests also have the opportunity to support local artisans and small businesses while enjoying food from North Shore vendors before or after the presentation. Together, the evening celebrates the rich diversity of Polynesian cultures while honoring the traditions and heritage of Hawaiʻi.

By the conclusion of the Talk Story session, participants leave with a deeper appreciation for Hawaiian and Polynesian culture, stronger connections with the local community, and lasting memories of an evening centered on storytelling, hospitality, and aloha. The experience reflects Marriott's commitment to offering meaningful cultural programming that enriches every guest's visit while supporting local practitioners and community leaders in preserving Hawaiʻi's living traditions.

title: Mālama ʻĀina Workday
teaser:
Step beyond sightseeing and experience Hawaiʻi through meaningful service during a guided Mālama ʻĀina Workday at Kaluanui. Led by cultural practitioners and community stewards, this hands-on experience invites guests to actively participate in the care and restoration of a culturally significant landscape while gaining a deeper understanding of the Hawaiian relationship between people and the land.

The workday begins with a welcome and cultural orientation, introducing participants to the history of Kaluanui, its importance within Koʻolauloa, and the Hawaiian values that guide stewardship of the ʻāina. Guests learn that mālama ʻāina—caring for the land—is more than conservation; it is a reciprocal relationship rooted in gratitude, responsibility, and the understanding that when we care for the land, the land cares for us.

Throughout the experience, participants work alongside local cultural practitioners on projects that directly support the ongoing restoration and preservation of the area. Activities may include removing invasive species, planting native vegetation, maintaining mala and agricultural spaces, clearing trails, revitalizing cultural sites, or assisting with other seasonal stewardship efforts. Each workday is tailored to the current needs of the ʻāina, ensuring that every participant contributes to meaningful, lasting improvements.

As guests work, cultural practitioners share stories, history, and traditional ecological knowledge that connect each task to the broader Hawaiian worldview. Participants gain insight into native plants, traditional land management practices, watershed restoration, sustainable agriculture, and the enduring importance of caring for places that have nourished Hawaiian communities for generations.

The experience encourages collaboration, reflection, and genuine cultural exchange. Guests are welcome to ask questions, engage with local stewards, and learn firsthand how community-led stewardship efforts continue to protect Hawaiʻi's natural and cultural resources for future generations.

Following the workday, guests are invited to relax and enjoy light refreshments while continuing conversations with the cultural practitioners and fellow participants. This informal gathering provides an opportunity to reflect on the day's experience, ask additional questions, and strengthen the connections formed through shared stewardship.

By the conclusion of the workday, participants leave with more than the satisfaction of volunteering. They depart with a deeper appreciation for Hawaiʻi's cultural values, a stronger connection to the land and its people, and the knowledge that their efforts have contributed to the continued restoration of Kaluanui. This experience embodies the true spirit of mālama ʻāina, transforming visitors into active participants in preserving Hawaiʻi's living heritage while creating memories that extend far beyond their time in the islands.

title: THE MOTH 2026
teaser:
One foot in front of another…

Join The Moth this fall for TIGHTROPE, an evening of extraordinary true stories about what happens when there's no clear path—only the courage to keep moving forward.

Stories of balancing without a net. Trusting your gut. Taking the leap before you know where you'll land. Of big gambles and near misses, quiet acts of bravery and glorious mistakes. Of sending the text, booking the flight, sharing the secret you've carried for years, and watching everything change.

The Mainstage tour is The Moth’s signature live show, featuring a carefully curated lineup of tellers—writers, artists, adventurers, community members, and unexpected voices—sharing true personal stories, told live and without notes.

Come spend an evening on the edge. One step can change the whole story.

Sponsored by the Hawai'i Tourism Authority  
  
About The Moth: 

The Moth is a global storytelling nonprofit with the mission to inspire people to listen and share openly, think and feel deeply, and expand their understanding of one another. Since 1997, The Moth has presented more than 70,000 true stories—told live and without notes—in 11 countries, across 4 continents. Today, The Moth produces 600+ live shows annually, as well as the Peabody Award-winning The Moth Radio Hour, and the popular The Moth Podcast. Through workshops for students, educators, adults, advocates, and professionals, The Moth guides thousands of new storytellers each year in finding and sharing their own voices. Learn more at themoth.org @MothStories

title: Nature in Harmony: Music and Nature Journaling at Mānoa Heritage Center
teaser:
Thursday, September 24  
6:00 pm - 8:00 pm  
Mini-concert and Nature Journaling experience: $35

Music, art, and nature can deepen our experience of the world around us.

Inspired by Carnival of the Nearly Extinct Animals, this special collaboration between Mānoa Heritage Center and Ocean Music Action invites participants to celebrate Hawaiʻi's remarkable biodiversity through live music, exploration, and hands-on art making.

The evening begins with a musical performance featuring harpist Megan Conley, bassist Shawn Conley, and violinist Iggy Jang. The program will feature music by inspired by the ﬂora and fauna of Hawaii, including whales, butterﬂies, and kāhuli.

Following the performance, local artist and naturalist Kate Righter will lead a guided nature journaling experience through the beautiful gardens of Mānoa Heritage Center. Participants will observe native plants that provide food and habitat for Hawaiʻi's endangered species—including ʻōhiʻa and māmaki—and will be guided in the creation of their own nature journal pages, while learning how careful observation through writing and drawing can foster a deeper appreciation for the natural world.

This unique experience offers an opportunity to engage the senses— to listen, look closely, and deepen our understanding of the beauty and interconnectedness of Hawaiʻi's living landscapes.

Advance registration required; space is limited to 20 participants. 

About the Artists: 

Megan Conley grew up in Austin, Texas, and began playing harp at age 5. By age 15 she had performed on the Grammy Award-winning album. 'Los Super Seven.' She was awarded a Fulbright Grant to study music in Paris, France, and in 2012 she won first place in the International Ima Hogg Concerto Competition. 

Megan served as Principal Harpist of the Houston Symphony from 2015-2022. She is the harpist of the NYC-based orchestra The Knights, and has performed at Lincoln Center and Carnegie Hall with the New York City Ballet among others. 

In 2021, Megan founded Ocean Music Action, a nonproﬁt that uses music to build community and promote action for ocean conservation.

Learn more at: Ocean Music Action 

Kate Righter grew up in both Kailua and Virginia, exploring forests and tide pools, taking art classes, and writing stories and poetry.

After graduating from Virginia Tech in 2005, Kate returned to Hawaiʻi, where she worked as both a graphic designer and an elementary school art teacher. In 2022, she founded the Hawaiʻi Nature Journal Club, connecting people through nature journaling, environmental stewardship, and creativity.

Kate is a certiﬁed Nature Journal Educator through the Wild Wonder Foundation and leads workshops for schools, nonproﬁts, and community groups throughout Hawaiʻi. 

Kate is also an artist and poet. She is creating a series of paintings inspired by Hawaiʻi’s coastal species and is the author of What Remains, a collection of poetry and essays inspired by nature and family life.

title: Waipā Food and Farm Tour
teaser:
Join us on an unforgettable learning journey through Waipā, a lush 1,600 acre river valley on Kaua`iʻs north shore. Waipā valley is a traditional Hawaiian land division known as an ahupua`a, which i ka wā kahiko (in ancient times) supported a sustainable and thriving community of potentially over a thousand people.

Many of the valuable features of the ancient irrigation and field systems and Halulu fishpond continue to exist today, having been restored and maintained by the Waipā Foundation over the last 30 years. The historic auwai, or irrigation canal, continues to bring water to a network of gardens, orchards and agroforestry plantings as it did in the time of our ancestors. Today, these farms and gardens provide increasing amounts of food for the local community and Waipāʻs educational programs.

Walk and ride from the coastline at Hanalei bay to the cool uplands of Waipā stream exploring the ecosystems that support our food plants, native wildlife and the invasive species that challenge them. All while learning about the traditional values and practices which ensured the sustainability of our people and how we are adapting and applying them along with modern tools and technology.

This experience will change the way you view Hawai`iʻs natural landscapes and environment, knowing the cultural features and significance that lie within them.

Tours run Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays 9am-12:30pm and include a continental breakfast upon arrival, a tasting along the way, and a four course lunch with ingredients mostly sourced from Waipā.

title: 19th Annual Run for the Dry Forest
teaser:
Join us for the 19th annual Run for the Dry Forest at the Puʻuwaʻawaʻa Forest Reserve! 

Featuring a 10K run, a 5K run/walk, and two keiki runs, this unique event offers the chance to explore a stunning landscape while directly supporting vital conservation efforts. Beyond the trails, enjoy outreach booths and a silent auction featuring amazing experiences and products generously donated by local businesses. It’s fun for the whole family!

Pu‘uwa‘awa‘a is a State-managed area that is one of very few intact examples of a Hawaiian dryland forest. Global estimates show tropical dry forests have been reduced to less than 5% of their previous coverage. Proceeds will be used for research and management at Pu‘uwa‘awa‘a and adjacent Pu‘uanahulu.

Race Options:

  * 10K Run: An "extreme trail running experience" with a challenging 1200 ft. elevation gain in the first 3 miles – perfect for experienced runners.



  * 5K Run/Walk: A scenic course suitable for all fitness levels and jogging strollers. This trail includes coarse rock, dirt, and paved sections and is suitable for most! Strollers with large wheels allowed.



  * Keiki Fun Runs: There will be two fun and easy races for kids and parents. A ¼ mile non-competitive run around the reservoir and a short keiki dash in the field.




Registration is required, and we encourage you to sign up early as prices will increase closer to race day. Please note, there will be no same-day registration.

To learn more and to register please go to akakaforests.org/run.

  


We are always looking for volunteers! Sign-up here to help us with our biggest event of the year! https://forms.gle/C5iT7Ss54HpS3agY7

title: JoAnn Conducts Beethoven's Triple

Returning to lead HSO, Conductor Emeritus JoAnn Falletta brings together three exceptional soloists—pianist Lisa Nakamichi, violinist Ignace Jang, and cellist Julian Schwarz—for Beethoven’s brilliant Triple Concerto, a rare and captivating work where three solo instruments come together in musical conversation.

The program continues with the Hawaiʻi premiere of Randall Svane’s Quantum Flight and Sibelius’ powerful Symphony No. 1, taking audiences on a journey from energetic modern sounds to sweeping romantic melodies.

title: ʻAha Kuauli Workshop Series
teaser:
A series of educational and cultural workshop for adults and young adults.   


The ʻAha Kuauli Workshop Series is a community-based cultural education initiative designed to extend the impact of the Hawaiʻi Kuauli Pacific & Asia Cultural Festival beyond its annual June celebration held in honor of King Kamehameha Day in Kailua-Kona, Hawaiʻi, at the Courtyard Marriott, Kona Beach Resort.

Taking place on November 6 & 7, 2026, at the Courtyard Marriott, Kona Beach Resort, ʻAha Kuauli will host an immersive series of four impactful, hands-on training workshops designed to educate, inspire, and empower participants across cultural and professional disciplines. These workshops will focus on:

  * Hawaiian Cultural Protocol Education  
Participants will gain ʻike Hawaiʻi by understanding the traditional Hawaiian practices, values, and protocols, cultivating cultural awareness and respect.

  * Fire-Knife Competition Education & Training  
Youth and adults from across the Hawaiian Islands will have the opportunity to learn and develop skills in fire-knife performance, emphasizing discipline, safety, and cultural significance in the history of Siva Afi Sāmoa.

  * Fashion Design Business Workshop  
Aspiring designers who are Hawaiʻi Island residents and enrolled in local schools will receive guidance on building and sustaining a fashion business, from concept development to branding and marketing. 

  * Culinary Arts Training & Practicum  
Students will engage in hands-on culinary training led by award-winning professional chefs, gaining valuable experience in food preparation, hospitality, and Pacific & Asian cultural cuisine.




The ʻAha Kuauli event aims to support and cultivate talent that preserves cultural tradition and provide career pathways for participants within the community at large. These workshops will provide fundamental opportunities for the workforce to equip the next generation of leaders in the Hawaiian Islands and create opportunities for local schools to engage in indigenous Native Hawaiian and Pacific cultural practices and lifestyles.

title: Carnival of the Nearly Extinct Animals
teaser:
This September, Ocean Music Action and Hawaiʻi Theatre Center invite audiences to discover a world of imagination where music, movement, and art reveal the beauty and wonder of some of our planet's most extraordinary animals. 

Making its World Premiere on Friday, September 18, at 7:30 p.m. and Saturday, September 19, at 3:00 p.m. at the historic Hawaiʻi Theatre, Carnival of the Nearly Extinct Animals is a visually stunning interdisciplinary performance inspired by Camille Saint-Saëns' beloved Carnival of the Animals and an original companion work by composer Stephanie Ann Boyd. 

Presented by Ocean Music Action in partnership with Hawaiʻi Theatre Center, the production brings together internationally recognized artists and leading local creatives in a one-of-a-kind collaboration. Dancers from the NYC company Dance Heginbotham join dancers of Ballet Hawaiʻi, pairing new choreography with live chamber music and larger-than-life puppetry by Obie Award-winning puppeteer Greg Corbino. Acclaimed Hawaiʻi actor and storyteller Moses Goods serves as narrator, with original poetry written by local students is woven throughout the performance. This immersive 1 hour 20 minute theatrical experience is designed for audiences of all ages.

By highlighting endangered animals from across the globe, Carnival of the Nearly Extinct Animals celebrates the beauty, diversity, and resilience of the natural world. Through imagination, creativity, and artistic collaboration, audiences encounter thirteen remarkable species—including whales, sea turtles, elephants, tigers, coral, bees and butterflies, black rhinos, bison, gray wolves, and kāhuli (land snails)—through music, dance, poetry, and puppetry.

"Art has a unique ability connect us, to open minds and hearts, and to express the inexpressible,” said Megan Conley, founder and president of Ocean Music Action. "Our hope is that audiences leave feeling inspired and empowered—filled with joy and wonder, and a desire to help protect these extraordinary animals and their habitats." 

The performances are the centerpiece of a month-long series of community events across Oʻahu developed in collaboration with leading cultural, educational, and conservation organizations. Programs include performances at local libraries, Community Sunday on Aug 16th the Honolulu Museum of Art, nature journaling at Mānoa Heritage Center, volunteer stewardship opportunities with Aloha Tree Alliance and Mālama Maunalua, and educational events at the Bishop Museum and East-West Center. 

Friday evening ticket holders are invited to arrive early for a pre-performance conversation featuring local experts discussing the animals highlighted in the production. Saturday afternoon audiences can enjoy an art-making activity before the performance. 

Tickets at hawaiitheatre.com/carnival

title: Drawing in Space - The Sculpted Line
teaser:
Drawing in Space — The Sculpted Line Instructor: Artist and educator Maya Lea Portner SAT OCT 3 and SAT OCT 10, 9:00 am - 2:00 pm* *Must be able to make both dates 2-day workshop: $50 

This is a workshop for artists of all levels to expand beyond the focus of pure technique and to develop new approaches in their work. Whether one is new to artmaking and seeking an experience to unlock creativity, or is a seasoned artist hoping to gain new “tools” to add to their studio practice, this course offers approaches to “making” that will last well beyond the duration of the workshop. 

The workshop comprises a series of exercises to stimulate artistic experimentation across 2- and 3- dimensions, borrowing techniques from millinery (hat making) wire construction, basketry, and drawing that will allow students to focus on the natural craft experience of “thinking with your hands”. Using the Hawaiian concept of kilo, participants will closely observe their surroundings and translate that experience into bent 18 gauge wire. An exercise that considers makawalu or "eight points-of-view" will be explored to create abstract drawings. Finally, we will explore the concept of kaona or "layered meanings" in our group reflection.

Participants will leave the workshop with strategies from both western art traditions and Hawaiian frameworks to stretch their imaginations. With ideas that are flexible to their individual materials, techniques and levels of expertise, all are invited to go beyond what was previously thought possible.

Maya Lea Portner is an artist and educator from Honolulu, Hawai‘i. Raised in Mānoa Valley, she earned a BFA (Sculpture) from Washington University School of Art in St. Louis and an MFA in Art (Fibers) at the University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa, where she was a student of Pat Hickman. She has been an instructor in art on O‘ahu for 20 years, and currently teaches at Leeward Community College, Pu‘uloa Campus. Her teaching, research and art exhibitions have taken her around the world: Italy, India, Senegal, Majuro Atoll (Micronesia), The Netherlands, Maine, Missouri, California and New York. Maya Portner is the 13th recipient of the prestigious Catherine E.B. Cox Award for Excellence in the Visual Arts, awarded biannually by the Honolulu Museum of Art.

You are joining a movement that celebrates Hawaiian heritage and traditions, while also recognizing the need to protect and preserve our precious natural resources. Together, we can transcend the role of mere visitors and become stewards of the land and sea, ensuring a vibrant and sustainable future for generations to come. 

E komo mai, come and journey with us as we share not just a place, but a way of life.

title: Auwahi greenhouse native plant work day
teaser:
Volunteer workdays at the Auwahi native tree nursery will be held each month. Due to the nature of this work and to assure safety on Ranch premises, volunteers are required to apply by sending an email to volunteer@auwahi.org and must be approved prior to participation. Approved volunteers will be given further information including the meet time, safety concerns, and the agenda for the day. Volunteers will work at the Auwahi native tree nursery to, together as a community, help restore Maui’s essential watershed forests. 

The day’s work will be broken into one and a half sessions with snacks, drinks, and talk story before heading back into another shorter session. During breaks, Auwahi staff will conduct short talks and show-and-tells with specific native plants and their usages to the ‘people of old’, and about the history of the Honua’ula moku, the ancient district in which ‘Ulupalakua Ranch is largely included. Though participants can leave as needed, in practice most participants spend the whole day here, even hanging around afterwards to continue talk story. Learning to identify and become kama`aina with native plants as elements of the Hawaiian landscape as well as learning the details and techniques of stewarding native forest recovery can have a powerful impact on people.

Participants for the E Kanu Kakou happenings will meet in the grass parking lot across from ‘Ulupalakua Ranch headquarters and just Kahului-side of the Ranch store and deli and from there be taken to the adjacent Auwahi native tree nursery area. On every E Kanu Kakou ‘happening’, Auwahi project staff will led an interpretive tour of the nursery area, giving visitors and residents unique insights into the way plants and lifestyles have interacted over the centuries of time here – first the Hawaiian culture, followed by the unique paniolo way of life that is retained to the present at `Ulupalakua Ranch – one of a handful of areas in the Hawaiian Islands where this culture is still alive and thriving.

title: Mele Tūtū – Songs of our Grandparents
teaser:
The Hawaiian Mission Houses Historic Site and Archives (HMH) invites the community to experience “Mele Tūtū: Songs of our Grandparents”, the next installment of HMH’s acclaimed Mele Program. “Mele Tūtū means to invite guests to look closely at the memories and songs of our grandparents or great-grandparents’ generation from the 1930s/1940s. Connection to our kūpuna, our elders, helps us to maintain the genealogies, histories, and mana of generations that we revere today. Expressed through mele (song), oli (chant), and hula (dance), Mele Tūtū embodies the enduring principle of Mālama Kūpuna: caring for our elders and those whose shoulders we all stand upon in our present-day lives.

In the 1930s and 1940s, during the time of our grandparents and great-grandparents, live music performances and radio broadcasts were important ways of sharing local music not only across the islands, but also to the Continental U.S. and further abroad. Radio shows like “Hawaiʻi Calls” and its descendant program in the 1970s and 1980s, “Territorial Airwaves” helped to broadcast Hawaiian music, mele, and culture to people otherwise unfamiliar with Hawaiʻi, its history, or its people. Orchestras playing hapahaole music, jazz, and other forms of popular Hawaiian music were instrumental in connecting people across the airwaves.

For many kamaʻāina, the mele and hula of the 1930s and 1940s are direct connections to their ancestors who danced hula, played in world-renowned touring Hawaiian bands, and kept the memory and music of previous generations alive in new contemporary ways for the time period. These mele and hula evoke memories of family musicians in the yard or on the lānai, at family gatherings, or times when kūpuna would share the knowledge and history of the family with the younger generations. It brings back memories of joy, happiness, fun, and genuine connection between family members.

title: U.S. Poet Laureate Arthur Sze in Conversation — Fri, Sept. 18
teaser:
This September, 25th United States poet laureate Arthur Sze will come to Honolulu for the first stop of his "Words Bridging Worlds" project, a four-city national tour encouraging Americans to engage with translation. Organized by the Library of Congress in collaboration with several Hawaiʻi nonprofit organizations, programming will take place across two consecutive days, with a public presentation on Friday, September 18 at Mission Memorial Auditorium and a translation workshop to follow on Saturday, September 19. These programs are both free and open to the public with pre-registration required. Registration is now available through The Library of Congress. This programming is being organized with the support and participation of several Hawaiʻi-based nonprofit organizations. These include The Merwin Conservancy—a Maui-based nonprofit organization founded to steward the home, garden, and legacy of the renowned poet and ecologist W.S. Merwin—where Arthur Sze was a resident in 2022. Arthur Sze’s public presentation at Mission Memorial Auditorium is made possible through the support of the Honolulu Mayor’s Office of Culture and the Arts. The Hawaiʻi Center for the Book, housed at the Hawaiʻi State Library, will host a translation workshop the following day, on September 19. Additional support for this program is provided by the Laila Twigg-Smith Art Fund.

The September 18th event will launch Arthur Sze’s “Words Bridging Worlds” tour, the main project of his second term as poet laureate which empowers readers to dissolve the boundaries between reading, writing, and translating poetry. Recognizing the Hawaiian Islands as a vital crossroads of cultural and linguistic exchange, and honoring the vitality and enduring presence of ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi, Arthur Sze will be in conversation with Puakea Nogelmeier, co-founder of Awaiaulu, an organization dedicated to fortifying the continuity of Hawaiian language and knowledge. Hawaiʻi State Poet Laureate Lee Tonouchi, Da Pidgin Guerrilla, will introduce the event, drawing a connection between the national and Hawaiʻi’s state laureateship, which is hosted by The Hawaiʻi State Foundation on Culture and the Arts, Hawaiʻi Council for the Humanities, and Hawaiʻi State Public Library System. On the afternoon of September 19th, a translation workshop will take place at the Hawaiʻi Center for the Book, allowing participants to practice their own translations.

title: THE EPIC TALE OF THE RAMAYANA
teaser:
A Hawaii Theatre production in partnership with the Still & Moving Meditation Fellowship + Still & Moving Community Center

Friday, November 6, 2026 · Pre-show talk 6:30 PM · Curtain 7:00 PM

For nearly two decades, Still & Moving has marked Diwali, the Indian festival of lights, with a living retelling the world's oldest epic: the Ramayana. What began as a small community gathering — a story shared among students and teachers — has grown into a full theatrical production, drawing dozens of performers ranging in age from 5 to 85. This year, for the first time, that story steps onto one of the most storied stages in the Pacific: the Hawaiʻi Theatre.

The Epic Tale of the Ramayana follows Prince Ram and Princess Sita, cast from their kingdom into exile, and the courage, loyalty, and love that carry them through it — including Sita's abduction by the ten-headed demon king Ravana, and her rescue by the troops Prince Ram and the devoted monkey-warrior Hanuman. At its heart, it's a story about the triumph of good over selfishness, light over darkness — the very themes Diwali itself celebrates.

What makes this production distinct is who tells it. Rather than a single dance tradition, the Ramayana is carried across many: Bharatanatyam and other Indian classical dances, hula, aerial arts, belly dance, samba, Argentine tango, and Brazilian capoeira, all performed by Still & Moving's own community of teachers, students, and staff. Many performers are stepping into a dramatic role for the first time in their lives — carried by narration that lets them fully inhabit a character without needing to memorize a single line. The result is less a staged play than a communal offering: a room full of different backgrounds and disciplines, telling one universal story together.

Bringing this beloved tradition to the Hawaiʻi Theatre — with its own century of history as a gathering place for Honolulu's arts and culture — marks a new chapter for Still & Moving Meditation Fellowship & Still & Moving Community Center, with an invitation for the wider community to witness and participate in this joyous annual celebration.

Join us Friday, November 6, 2026, for a pre-show talk at 6:30 PM offering context on the story and its traditions, with curtain at 7:00 PM.

title: Sansei Connections
teaser:
Sansei Artists ‘Connect’ on Many Levels

Four  
of Hawaii’s most accomplished artists will join in “Sansei Connections,” a very  
special art exhibition to be held at the Hawaii Japanese Center from September  
19 to November 14. The four featured artists are: ceramicist Clayton Amemiya;  
painter, printmaker and sculptor Hiroki Morinoue; sculptor and printmaker Lonny  
Tomono; and painter and printmaker Glenn Yamanoha.

Amemiya  
developed his craft in Okinawa, drawing inspiration from both Hawaii and Japan,  
Amemiya moved to the Big Island and built an anagama – a traditional  
Japanese wood-fired tunnel kiln – that would influence and define his artistic brilliance  
over the next five decades. 

Born  
in Hilo, Lonny Tomono completed a rigorous, five-year apprenticeship in Kyoto,  
Japan under master temple builder Seiichiro Kitamura. Tomono spent six days  
every week working on some of Japan’s most treasured temples, shrines and  
gardens. In the process, he learned the demanding traditions of Japanese  
carpentry, where every gesture embodies generations of accumulated knowledge. 

Hiroki  
Morinoue was born and raised in the coffee-growing community of Holualoa on the  
Kona side of Hawaii Island. Today, Morinoue is recognized internationally as  
both an accomplished abstract painter and master printmaker. Morinoue, his wife  
Setsuko, and daughters Miho and Maki, have devoted a lifelong commitment to  
community, including the establishment of the Donkey Mill Art Center that  
provides opportunities for future generations of local artists. 

Glenn  
Yamanoha studied traditional Japanese woodblock printing in Kyoto through a  
prestigious Monbusho scholarship. Japan transformed him both as an artist and  
as a person. Throughout his life, Yamanoha has embraced Japanese aesthetic  
principles such as wabi-sabi, which finds beauty in imperfection and  
impermanence.

“The title of this  
exhibition, Sansei Connections, speaks to more than ancestry. It suggests the  
many crossings that shape a life between Hawaii and Japan, tradition and  
innovation, nature and abstraction, artist and viewer.” — Glenn Yamanoha

All  
four artists will display work from early in their careers to the present.  
“Sansei Connections” is free and open to the public Wednesday to Saturday, 11  
a.m. to 3 p.m. (closed holidays) through November 14. Admission is free. For  
more information email info@hawaiijapanesecenter.com or call (808) 934-9611.

title: Kulāia Molokai
teaser:
Historical records dating back to 1865 note Hawaiian outrigger canoe race competitions as one of the many events our kūpuna took part in during annual lā kulāia, which are days of festivities honoring the Kingdom of Hawai‘i and especially honoring our beloved monarchy. During the Hawaiian Kingdom era, kulāia festivities generally occurred once a year during a national holiday or birthday celebration of mō‘i or monarch.​  
  
Subsequently after the overthrow of our beloved Hawaiian Kingdom, kulāia festivities changed focus and no longer celebrated the Kingdom and monarchy. In historical records, we see the shift from national celebration to simply canoe race competitions. Therefore, pieces of our historic kulāia were lost and forgotten.  
​  
In remembering the early years of the Moloka‘i Hoe along with the Aloha Festivals Ho‘olaule‘a at Hale O Lono, it was Moloka‘i’s version of the historic kulāia. The festivities lasted an entire weekend with campsites stretching from one end of Hale O Lono to the other and the spirit of ‘ohana and aloha radiated to all; including the various Moloka‘i ‘ohana, paddlers, visitors, spectators, and many others who came from the neighbor islands, outer states and other countries.  
​  
In recent years, we have seen history repeated, where the legacy of kulāia was forgotten, as the canoe races on Moloka'i continued without the festivals. Wanting to revive the spirit of the festivals here on Moloka‘i, a grassroots community group came together and formed the Moloka‘i Canoe Festivals Committee whose members share the vision of bringing back the festivals to our community and sharing the true Moloka‘i aloha and hospitality to our visiting brothers and sisters of the paddling ‘ohana. This practice of kulāia is an important cultural tradition that connects us to our ali‘i and our kūpuna. Kulāia gives us an opportunity to enlighten, embrace and share with those who visit our island about our values and resources we cherish which is our life source that sustains us and keeps Moloka‘i, Moloka‘i. May we embrace this valuable tradition and pass it down to our own keiki and mo‘opuna for generations to come.

title: Molokai Farmers Market
teaser:
The Molokai Farmers Market Returns — Right Back Where It Belongs

Restoring a Tradition in the Heart of Kaunakakai  
  
For years, the Molokai Farmers Market was a Saturday morning tradition in Kaunakakai — a gathering place where farmers, food vendors, and artisans came together to share their harvests, crafts, and aloha. Every weekend, the lot at Molokai Center came alive with music, laughter, and the scent of local food filling the air.  
  
But when COVID-19 hit, everything changed.  
  
Like many community markets across Hawai‘i, the Molokai Farmers Market had to close for public safety. What was once a thriving hub of community connection fell silent. In the years that followed, as smaller markets appeared around the island, vendors noticed that the crowds never quite returned.  
  
Former vendors from the old market began reaching out, expressing their desire to come back to town — back to the heart of Kaunakakai, where the community could easily gather and where local businesses could benefit from the energy of market day.  
  
Nearby shops along Ala Malama Avenue echoed that call, remembering how the weekly market brought steady foot traffic and life to the downtown area.  
  
Recognizing that need, Pūlama Ka Heke took on a mission to restore the Molokai Farmers Market to town. The team reached out to Molokai Center to discuss how they could collaborate to support local vendors and strengthen Molokai’s economic heartbeat once again.  
  
As discussions evolved, Market Manager Tylor Tanaka proposed a simple but powerful idea: to host the market on the Molokai Public Library lawn — conveniently located right across the street from the original farmers market site.  
  
The location was symbolic — close to the market’s roots and perfectly positioned for families, kupuna, and visitors to gather again. Tylor met with Librarian Mia Ritte, who shared the same vision of using the library lawn as a community gathering space that supports local culture, agriculture, and entrepreneurship.  
  
Together, they formed a partnership built on aloha, collaboration, and purpose.  
  
Now, with support from the County of Maui Office of Economic Development, the Molokai Farmers Market is returning to town — stronger and more community-driven than ever.  
  
The market’s revival is more than just reopening; it’s a homecoming.  
A homecoming for our vendors, our community, and the spirit of Molokai itself.

title: Courtyard by Marriott Oahu North Shore Talk Story: Steve Sue of Talk Shaka
teaser:
The Courtyard Marriott Oahu North Shore invites the community to its upcoming Talk Story & Makeke event on Wednesday, September 23, 2026, featuring Steve Sue of Talk Shaka. Free and open to the public, the bi-monthly Talk Story & Makeke program provides a welcoming space to celebrate Hawaii’s people, stories and community while supporting local makers and small businesses. 

Sue is a Hawaiʻi filmmaker, storyteller and social entrepreneur best known as the producer and writer of “Shaka, A Story of Aloha,” an award-winning documentary exploring the origins, history and meanings of Hawaii’s iconic shaka gesture. What began as an effort to preserve the oral histories of Lāʻie kūpuna grew into a five-year journey examining more than a century of shaka history and the values of aloha represented by the gesture. His work ultimately grew beyond the film into Project Shaka, a nonprofit movement dedicated to sharing aloha and the values behind the gesture. Sue also wrote the 2024 legislation that established the shaka as the Official State Gesture of Hawaii and helped create the Hawaii DMV Shaka License Plate program. He currently serves as chairperson of ID8, the Hawaii nonprofit behind Project Shaka. 

During “Talk Shaka,” Sue will share the fascinating story behind one of Hawaii’s most recognizable symbols, including its deep connections to Lāʻie and Oahu’s North Shore. His documentary research began after he traveled to Lāʻie and met with kūpuna who wanted their stories preserved for future generations. In 2019, Sue recorded oral histories from six kūpuna, beginning the project that would eventually become Shaka, A Story of Aloha. 

Guests will have an opportunity to learn more about the history and meaning of the shaka and how a simple hand gesture has become a powerful expression of connection, kindness and aloha recognized around the world.

While there, guests can explore the “Hauoli Makeke,” a vibrant marketplace in the hotel’s courtyard featuring handmade goods and cultural creations. Offerings include Samoan weaving, Tahitian art, locally crafted jewelry, Tongan apparel, and more from talented local artisans and entrepreneurs. Past vendors have included Hailama Designs, Koa Jewelry, MELT Massage, and Shogo’s Gift Shop.

title: Keiki Construction Zone hosted by Bz Services LLC
teaser:
Keiki Construction Zone – Building the Future of Hawaiʻi

Keiki Construction Zone is Hawaiʻi’s only hands‑on jobsite built just for kids — a place where keiki can climb into real machinery, learn from industry pros, and discover how construction and agriculture work together to shape our islands. This event blends heavy equipment, farming education, and community pride into one unforgettable ʻohana experience.

A Real Jobsite for Real Learning

Inside the Keiki Construction Zone, children step into a safe, supervised environment filled with interactive stations and guided activities:

  * Mini Excavators & Rollers Keiki operate real equipment, dig, scoop, and roll under the guidance of trained professionals.

  * Big Rigz Exploration Area Climb into the cab, check out controls, and see how Hawaiʻi’s work trucks support our communities every day.

  * Agriculture Learning Zone Meet local farmers, land stewards, and ag practitioners who teach keiki about soil health, irrigation, composting, crop care, and the tools used to grow food across Hawaiʻi.

  * Farm Equipment Demonstrations See how tractors, attachments, and ag machinery help with planting, harvesting, and maintaining healthy land.

  * Hands‑On Building Stations Hammering, stacking, measuring, and simple construction tasks that spark imagination and build confidence.


Fun & Learning for the Whole ʻOhana

Families enjoy a full day of activities including:

  * Free bounce houses

  * Live entertainment

  * Food, treats, and local vendors

  * Community partners sharing resources, safety education, and giveaways


Inspiring Tomorrow’s Builders & Farmers

Keiki Construction Zone is more than an event — it’s a pathway. By connecting keiki with real operators, farmers, and industry practitioners, we help them see the future they can build with their own hands. It’s a celebration of Hawaiʻi’s workforce, our land, and the next generation who will care for both.

title: Designing the Pacific: Conversations Shaping the Future of Pacific Fashion
teaser:
Designing the Pacific brings working designers and makers into direct conversation with leaders from business, education, government, and philanthropy to consider what Pacific fashion needs to thrive.

Designed around exchange rather than formal presentations, the gathering will explore the cultural, economic, and practical questions shaping the future of fashion across Hawaiʻi and Oceania. Participants will gather in the round to share experience, identify industry needs, and consider what designers, educators, funders, businesses, and public partners might build together.

The goal is not to solve everything in one day. It is to deepen understanding, form new relationships, identify shared priorities, and create momentum for continued collaboration.

Program Schedule

10:00 a.m. — Welina  
Welcome and introduction to the day.

10:15 a.m. — Inheritance + Innovation  
Culture, Creativity, and Creative Ownership.  
FEATURED CONVERSATION PARTNER: Shar Tui'asoa of Punky Aloha Studio  
How do designers draw from inherited knowledge while creating new work, protecting cultural expression, and defining their own creative futures?

11:10 a.m. — Creativity + Commerce  
Capacity, Production, and Sustainable Growth  
FEATURED CONVERSATION PARTNER: Zach Pang of Manaola Hawai'i  
A practical look at the production, manufacturing, workforce, financing, and market access needed to build sustainable fashion businesses in Hawaiʻi and across Oceania.

12:05 p.m. — Conversations Around the Table  
Lunch and an opportunity to continue the exchange, build relationships, and explore areas of shared interest.

12:50 p.m. — Vision + Action  
Building the Pacific Creative Economy  
FEATURED CONVERSATION PARTNER: Karen Ewald of Hawai'i State Foundation on Culture and the Arts  
Participants identify shared priorities, potential collaborations, and what comes next for Pacific fashion and the wider creative economy.

1:45 p.m. — What We Carry Forward  
Closing reflections, shared priorities, and a pathway for continued collaboration.

2:00 p.m. — Pau
